scenes.title: Two taps, one order?
text: A customer taps Pay, the page hangs, and they tap it again.
Do they get charged twice?
This walkthrough follows one order through the Acme checkout design to answer that.
We'll trace the request, look at the change that makes retries safe, break a few dependencies, and finish with what's still open.

scenes.title: The path of a request
text: Let's start with the path a request takes.
It enters at the API gateway, which checks who you are and how fast you're calling.
Next, the order service validates the cart and reserves the stock.
Then the database records the order, exactly once.
Now watch one request travel all the way down, and the confirmation come back up.

scenes.title: The change that makes retries safe
text: Here's the part of the design that answers our question.
Before, every retry inserted a brand new order.
Now each request carries an idempotency key, created once by the client.
If that key was already used, the service returns the original order instead of writing a second one.
So two taps make one order, and one charge.

scenes.title: Failures stay contained
text: What happens when a dependency breaks?
If the cache goes down, reads get slower, but every order still goes through.
If a database replica fails, the primary keeps taking writes.
And if the payment provider times out, the charge waits in a queue and retries, instead of failing the order.

scenes.title: Agreeing across services
text: Placing an order touches three services, so they have to agree.
First, the coordinator asks every service to prepare.
Each one holds what it needs, but doesn't commit anything yet.
Once all three say they're ready, the coordinator tells them to commit, all together.
And if any one of them says no, everyone aborts, so nothing is ever half done.

scenes.title: The life of an order
text: Every order moves through a small set of states.
It starts as pending, and becomes paid once the charge clears.
From paid, it ships, and finally it's delivered.
At any point before shipping, it can be cancelled instead.
Delivered and cancelled are final. Once an order lands in one, it never moves again.

scenes.title: Where this is headed
text: So where is this headed?
In Q1 2027, payments moves into its own service.
In the second, checkout runs in a second region.
In the third, customers can edit an order after placing it.
And by the end of the year, the old monolith is retired.

scenes.title: What to check
text: Before you sign off, here's what the design settles, and what it leaves open.
One decision: the client creates the idempotency key, not the server.
The double tap has a test. Two requests with one key make exactly one order.
What isn't covered yet is two taps landing in different regions.
And the doc doesn't say how long a key is remembered. That's an open question.
Those last two are where your review time is best spent.

scenes.title: Recap
text: So, two taps, one order.
Every request carries a key, failures slow things down instead of failing the order, and two questions are still open.
Everything in this video comes from the Acme checkout design doc, revision four.
Thanks for watching.
